summary: Deprecates MD5-based authentication for the Network Time Protocol, because MD5 is considered too weak, and recommends AES-CMAC (RFC 4493) as a replacement for the message authentication code. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Time servers can sign their messages so nobody can fake them. The old signing method has become weak, so this document recommends a stronger one.

questions: why is md5 deprecated for ntp
subtitle: NTP packet authentication moves from MD5 to AES-CMAC, because MD5 is not a secure MAC.

tldr.problem: NTP authenticated packets by hashing the data with a 128-bit key using MD5, which is not a secure message authentication code.
tldr.mechanism: MD5-based authentication is deprecated. When NTP authentication is used, AES-CMAC with a 128-bit AES key is computed over the NTP header and any extension fields.
tldr.outcome: Hosts share a symmetric key out of band and old implementations without AES-CMAC cannot use such keys. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 5905 and is updated by RFC 9748.

today: RFC 8573 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5905 and is itself updated by RFC 9748.

sections.title: Why MD5 Goes
sections.content: RFC 5905 says NTP packets should be authenticated by appending the NTP data to a 128-bit key and hashing with MD5 to make a 128-bit tag. RFC 8573 says that, as discussed in the cited research and in RFC 6151, this is not a secure MAC and therefore MUST be deprecated.
sections.eli5: The old stamp can be copied by clever people, so we stop using it.

sections.title: AES-CMAC as the Replacement
sections.content:
If NTP authentication is implemented, AES-CMAC as specified in RFC 4493 MUST be computed over all fields in the NTP header and any extension fields present. The MAC key MUST be a 128-bit AES-128 key, and the resulting tag MUST be at least 128 bits long.

NTP can make this transition because it supports algorithm agility, as described in RFC 7696.
sections.eli5: The new stamp uses a secret key that only the two clocks know, and it covers the whole message.

sections.title: Shared Keys
sections.content:
Hosts that want NTP authentication share a symmetric key out of band, and MUST implement AES-CMAC. A key is a triplet of ID, type (for example MD5 or AES-CMAC) and the key itself, and all three must match for packets between two hosts to authenticate.

Old implementations that do not support AES-CMAC will not accept and will not send packets authenticated with such a key.
sections.eli5: Both clocks must hold the same secret, with the same name and the same kind of stamp, or they will not trust each other.

sections.title: Why AES-CMAC and Where to Look
sections.content:
The RFC gives four reasons: it is an IETF specification supported in many open source implementations; it is immune to nonce-reuse vulnerabilities because it uses no nonce; it has fine latency and throughput; and it benefits from native hardware support, such as Intel's New Instruction set.

Test vectors are in Section 4 of RFC 4493. There are no IANA actions. Security discussion is left to the NIST CMAC document and the security considerations of RFC 4493.
sections.eli5: It is a well-known method, it does not need a throwaway number that could be reused by mistake, and computers can do it quickly.
